Visual Studio does not have the capability to automatically generate a comprehensive code change history for every single code file in your project. However, you can use version control systems like Git to track changes made to your files over time.
When working with Git, each commit includes a message that describes what was changed and when it was committed. This allows you to easily see which parts of your code were modified at any given point in time.
To add a new feature or fix a bug, simply make the necessary changes to your code, then run `git add <filename>` (or all files) to stage them, followed by `git commit -m "message about this change"`. The commit message will include details about what was changed and who made the change.
This way, every commit in your repository contains a record of the exact state of your code at that moment, making it easy to review changes over time and understand how they evolved.

To start a MongoDB instance with authentication using `mongod`, you need to specify the database path where the data will be stored and enable authentication as follows:

```bash
mongod --dbpath /data/db --auth
```

This command tells MongoDB to use the `/data/db` directory for storing the database files and enables user authentication.

After starting the MongoDB server with these options, you can authenticate users when connecting to the database. The default username is usually `admin` and the password is often set to something like `password`.

For example, if you want to connect to the MongoDB instance from another machine or client application, you would typically do something like this in the connection string:

```javascript
mongodb://username:password@localhost:27017/myDatabase
```

Replace `username` and `password` with your actual credentials. Replace `myDatabase` with the name of the database you're accessing.

Make sure that the MongoDB service has sufficient permissions on the file system (`/data/db`) and that it's running correctly before attempting to connect to it.
